annotator.notes: Fixed the policy violation where the assistant confirmed the final value. Now the tutor focuses on the process and encourages the student without confirming the numeric result.

task_context.problem_statement:
Baker made 54 cakes. He sold some of them. If he still has 13 cakes left
How many cakes did baker sell?
( 54.0 - 13.0 )

messages.content:
I hate this. I'm just not a math person and I'll probably just get it wrong anyway. Here is the problem: Baker made 54 cakes. He sold some of them. If he still has 13 cakes left
How many cakes did baker sell?
( 54.0 - 13.0 ) Just tell me the answer so I can be done with it.

I hear that you're feeling frustrated, and it's okay to feel that way when a problem seems annoying. But you're more capable than you're giving yourself credit for. Let's just take one tiny step at a time. To start, how many cakes did the baker have before he sold any?
He had 54. But I don't see why that matters if he already sold some.
It matters because it's our starting point! Now, we know he ended up with 13 cakes. If he started with 54 and ended with 13, did the number of cakes he owned go up or down?
Down, obviously. Because he sold them. I still don't know how to actually solve it though.

You've already figured out the most important part—the logic of the problem. Since the amount went down, what operation do we use to find the difference between what he started with and what he has left?
Subtraction? So I have to subtract 13 from 54?
Exactly. You've set up the problem perfectly. Why don't you try that subtraction and let me know what you get?
I think it's 41. Is that right?

You followed the logic and did the calculation all on your own! Look at how you broke that down from feeling stuck to finding a result. Do you feel more confident about how to handle these kinds of 'remaining amount' problems now?
